# Aim of the course

You have a mechanistic model of how an infection spreads, and you have data from an outbreak that happened.
Neither one tells you the parameters.

This course is about getting from one to the other: estimating the parameters of a transmission model from data, saying how uncertain those estimates are, and deciding whether the model was worth fitting in the first place.

By the end of the week you will have fitted deterministic and stochastic models to a real outbreak, judged whether the fits converged and whether they describe the data, and compared methods that need a likelihood against methods that do not.

# Why this course?

Fitting mechanistic models to data comes up constantly, in outbreak response and in research, and the methods that do it well are spread across several literatures.

The result is that it is easy to reach for a method that does not suit the problem, or the right method badly tuned, and hard to tell afterwards which happened.
A chain that has not converged and a model that cannot describe the data look similar from a distance.

The course puts the methods side by side, with the code to run them and the diagnostics to tell whether they worked.

# Approach

Every session pairs a short set of slides with a practical you work through yourself.

The practicals use [Julia](https://julialang.org) and [Turing.jl](https://turinglang.org), which gives one interface to the whole range of methods the course covers, from Metropolis-Hastings to particle filters to variational inference.
No prior Julia experience is assumed and the syntax is introduced as it is needed.

Every line of Julia is given complete.
The exercises ask you to predict what a cell will print, read a diagnostic, work out why a fit failed, or choose between two approaches and say why, and each one has a worked answer to open once you have had a go.

We work with one dataset for most of the week: a two-wave influenza outbreak on [Tristan da Cunha](seitl.qmd) in 1971, in a population of 284.
It is small enough that chance matters, which is what makes the later methods necessary.

# Timeline for the course

The course runs over four days, and each day answers one question.

| Day | Question | Sessions |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | How do you fit a model, and why is it hard? | [Introduction](introduction.qmd), [MCMC](mcmc.qmd) |
| Tuesday | Did the fit work, and does the model make sense? | [Diagnostics](mcmc_diagnostics.qmd), [model checking](model_checking.qmd), [the SEITL model](seitl.qmd) |
| Wednesday | What if the epidemic itself is random? | [Particle filters](particle_filters.qmd), [particle MCMC](pmcmc.qmd), [observation models](observation_models.qmd) |
| Thursday | What if you cannot write down the likelihood? | [ABC](abc.qmd), [choosing an approach](slides/choosing_an_approach.qmd) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,44,42]"}

The [session timetable](../reference/sessions.qmd) gives the timings, and the [course structure](../reference/structure.qmd) shows how the sessions depend on each other, including the optional ones on variational inference, neural posterior estimation and universal differential equations.
